Chapter 4: How Beginnings, Middles, and Endings Shape Behavior.
Have you ever noticed how every project, relationship, or even a big life change always has a beginning, a middle, and an end? These aren’t just points on a calendar—they each play a unique role in how we feel, stay motivated, and ultimately, how satisfied we are.
Let’s start with beginnings. Think about your first day at a new job, or that moment you walk into a room full of strangers. The way things begin really sets the tone. A strong start can give you a boost of confidence and help you commit, while a shaky beginning might make you second-guess yourself or lose interest. This applies everywhere—even kids who start the school year feeling like they belong are more likely to do well.
But here’s the thing—not every beginning is up to us. Sometimes, after a setback, we need a reset. And research shows we’re more likely to make positive changes at what psychologists call “temporal landmarks.” These are moments that feel like a fresh start—like a birthday, the start of a week, or even New Year’s Day. They give us a mental clean slate, making it just a little bit easier to shake off old habits and set new goals.
Now, let’s talk about middles. People often overlook this stage, but it’s where things can get tricky. Ever notice how motivation can fade right around the halfway mark of a project or goal? That’s the “midpoint slump.” You might lose sight of your original excitement, get buried in the details, or just feel stuck. This isn’t just in your head—it happens with group projects, personal goals, you name it.
But the middle can also be a turning point. If you call out that halfway moment, it can actually wake you up. It’s a chance to pause, refocus, and adjust your strategy so you can rally and push through to the end. Teams that recognize and use that midpoint usually do better than those who just ignore it.
And then there are endings. The way something wraps up can completely shape how we remember the whole experience. A great ending leaves you feeling satisfied. But if things finish on a sour note, it can overshadow everything that came before. That’s why we often remember the last moments of a vacation or the final scene of a movie so clearly.
Endings also have this special power to light a fire under us. As a deadline gets closer, motivation often jumps up—a rush that helps us push through and finish strong. This “end spurt” can be a secret weapon against procrastination.
So, what can you do with all this? Here are a few practical ideas:
Start new projects or habits at meaningful moments, like the first day of the month or right after a big milestone. When you’re in the middle of something, pause and recognize that halfway point—use it as a chance to regroup and re-energize. And always plan for a strong finish. Celebrate what you’ve accomplished and take a moment to reflect on what you’ve learned.
When you really understand how beginnings, middles, and endings work on your mind, you can design your projects, routines, and experiences to keep your motivation high and make every ending as positive as possible.
